strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: future-frame extrapolation for dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes without requiring hand-specified forces, materials, or governing equations.

The proposed combination of a global/local latent representation, continuous Neural-ODE evolution, and Gaussian deformation decoding is coherent and can render arbitrary timestamps within a unified 3DGS framework.

The synthetic results are strong: ParticleGS substantially improves most extrapolation metrics on the Dynamic Objects and Dynamic Indoor Scene benchmarks while retaining broadly competitive reconstruction quality.
The evaluation includes reconstruction and extrapolation results, synthetic and real-world scenes, multiple NeRF/3DGS/physics-oriented baselines, qualitative comparisons, and component ablations.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is overstated. Only a single global feature is evolved by the Neural ODE, while particle-local features remain fixed; the decoder then maps this global trajectory and static spatial features to deformation. This is closer to a continuous time-conditioned deformation model than demonstrated learning of differential equations governing individual Gaussian-particle dynamics. No learned vector fields, conservation behavior, stability, or physical plausibility are analyzed.

The experiments train a separate model on the initial portion of each scene and extrapolate the same trajectory. They therefore establish per-sequence temporal curve extrapolation, not the claimed general ability to infer dynamics from observations. There is no evaluation on unseen scenes, motion instances, initial conditions, extrapolation horizons, or changed sampling rates, and the paper itself acknowledges the absence of motion generalization.

Real-world evidence is mixed rather than a significant overall improvement. On PanopticSports, ParticleGS gains only about 0.28 dB PSNR on average over GSPrediction, loses on Tennis PSNR, ties on Basketball PSNR, and has worse extrapolation LPIPS on all six sequences. Testing only timestamps after 0.9 also evaluates a very short horizon, with no error-versus-horizon analysis.

The ablations do not isolate the main scientific choices adequately. Removing the entire latent space creates a severely weakened model, while removing the Neural ODE causes only modest average changes. There is no comparison against a parameter-matched time-MLP, discrete latent update, polynomial trajectory, per-particle ODE, or alternative ODE solver, so it remains unclear whether continuous dynamics modeling is responsible for the gains.

The evidence for physical or stable motion is limited to image metrics and selected visualizations. No trajectory, flow, geometry, temporal-consistency, or long-horizon stability metric is reported, despite the paper noting that image metrics confound reconstruction and dynamics quality. Claims that affine decoding is physically plausible and improves geometry are consequently speculative.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the stated code link is blank, and important details such as latent dimensions, hash-grid resolutions and level count, FPS/KNN group sizes, ODE integration interval and step configuration, exact dataset frames/views, baseline tuning, runtime, and model size are missing. The affine decomposition mentioned in the appendix is also not formally specified.

Originality is moderate. Neural ODEs for continuous 4D representations and latent dynamics are established ideas, while the particle interpretation does not introduce particle interactions or particle-level state evolution. The related-work assertions that GNNs cannot represent temporal system evolution and that prior Neural-ODE methods cannot learn motion from videos are too categorical and insufficiently supported.

Several presentation and reporting issues reduce confidence: no aggregate results or uncertainty across runs are provided, statistical significance is not established, some numerical discussion does not match the tables, and there are apparent table/terminology errors such as the anomalous Grid4D Bat LPIPS value and inconsistent “ParticleGS/ParticalGS” naming. These are secondary to the conceptual and evaluation limitations but should be corrected.

strengths: The problem—future-state extrapolation from multiview observations—is important and less studied than interpolation-based dynamic reconstruction.

The combination of 3D Gaussian Splatting, spatial hash/PointNet-style features, and continuous-time latent evolution is intuitive and potentially useful. The method is described in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/cded935afed04c6080e6bb67c20b74bb/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The synthetic experiments cover six dynamic objects and four indoor scenes, compare against reconstruction and extrapolation methods, and show substantial extrapolation gains on several cases, especially Shark, Whale, Telescope, Bat, and the indoor scenes.

Evaluation also includes six real PanopticSports sequences, and the ablation indicates that latent encoding is essential while the Neural ODE and affine decoder each provide smaller additional improvements.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning underlying physical dynamics is not established. Only one global vector g evolves under dg/dt=f(g,t), while every particle's local feature remains fixed. Because the vector field explicitly receives time and is optimized per scene, the model may simply fit a time-conditioned trajectory rather than discover a reusable dynamical law. No physical-state, trajectory, acceleration, conservation, or cross-scene generalization evaluation distinguishes these explanations.

The claim that the Neural ODE is responsible for extrapolation is inadequately controlled. The undefined “w/o Neural ODE” baseline is only modestly worse—34.224 versus 33.790 PSNR on Dynamic Objects and 29.772 versus 28.658 on Indoor Scenes—and there is no comparison with a similarly sized time-conditioned MLP, polynomial trajectory, recurrent model, or other continuous representation. Consequently, the benefit of the specific ODE formulation is unclear.

The real-world evidence is weak relative to the headline claim. PanopticSports reserves only the final 10% for short-horizon extrapolation and is deliberately selected so that motion remains predictable. ParticleGS is mixed against GaussianPrediction: it has slightly higher average PSNR and SSIM but consistently worse LPIPS on the reported sequences, with a PSNR tie on Basketball and a loss on Tennis. No longer-horizon or multiple-cutoff analysis is provided.

The formulation conflates per-scene trajectory continuation with general future prediction. Each scene is optimized for 50,000–80,000 steps, and the paper explicitly reports no generalization to unseen scenes or motions. Equation 3 nevertheless presents the task as estimating the most likely conditional future, although the deterministic method cannot represent multimodal futures or quantify uncertainty.

Several technical details are insufficient or questionable. Adding ΔR directly to a rotation matrix does not preserve a valid rotation; the appendix instead refers vaguely to decomposing transformations into rotation, scale, shear, velocity, and nonlinear terms without giving equations. The paper does not substantiate why independently decoded per-Gaussian affine parameters ensure structural or physical plausibility.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are limited: there are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, runtime/memory/model-size comparisons, baseline-training details, or sensitivity studies. Important implementation values such as latent dimensions, FPS/KNN counts, learning rates, ODE step/time normalization, and densification settings are missing. The stated code link is blank.

The ablation is not sufficiently diagnostic. Removing the entire latent space causes collapse but does not isolate global versus local encoding; removing affine deformation produces only small gains; and neither the global-state construction nor the claimed physically plausible parameter decomposition is separately evaluated.

The novelty is moderate rather than compelling: the method mainly combines established 3DGS deformation, hash/PointNet-style encoding, and Neural ODE components. The strong “first” and “prior-free” claims are overstated because the design still imposes substantial smoothness, global-latent, affine-motion, and deterministic-evolution priors.

Qualitative support is selective and difficult to assess: only isolated timestamps are shown, there is no real-world qualitative comparison, and no temporal videos, trajectories, or failure cases demonstrate long-term stability. These evidence gaps are material, whereas typographical errors and inconsistent naming such as ParticleGS/ParticalGS are secondary presentation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D scenes from visual observations without manually specified material models, forces, or governing equations. This is relevant to computer vision applications beyond interpolation-oriented dynamic reconstruction.

ParticleGS presents a coherent end-to-end design combining per-Gaussian hash features, a scene-level feature encoder, Neural ODE evolution, and an affine Gaussian deformation decoder. The approach is technically plausible and easy to integrate with 3D Gaussian Splatting.

The synthetic extrapolation results are compelling and broad enough to establish practical value. ParticleGS obtains the best extrapolation PSNR on all six Dynamic Object scenes and all four Dynamic Indoor scenes, often by large margins; for example, it reaches 38.17 versus 30.90 PSNR on Shark and 33.57 versus 25.42 on Factory.

Evaluation includes 16 scenes spanning synthetic objects, multi-object indoor scenes, and real captured human motion. Comparisons cover both reconstruction-focused methods and the more directly relevant NVFi and GaussianPrediction extrapolation baselines.

The real PanopticSports results provide additional, if more modest, support: ParticleGS has the best or tied extrapolation PSNR on five of six sequences and generally strong SSIM, showing that the approach is not confined to simple synthetic motion.

Qualitative examples support the quantitative results, particularly for rotating objects and multi-object indoor scenes, where ParticleGS often preserves object identity and future pose better than the baselines.

The ablations indicate that the latent representation is essential and that both ODE evolution and affine deformation contribute incremental improvements. Overall, the supported extrapolation gains and usefulness outweigh the reservations, motivating a weak accept.
weaknesses: Material concern: the paper overstates its interpretation as particle-level dynamics. Equation 6 evolves only a single global state g_t shared by the scene, while every Gaussian's local feature l remains fixed. Thus, there is no explicit particle-specific differential state or interaction dynamics; operationally, the method is closer to a globally time-conditioned deformation field than to a learned particle dynamics system.

Material concern: the ablation does not isolate the value of Neural ODEs convincingly. The undefined 'w/o Neural ODE' variant is already close to the full method—33.79 versus 34.22 extrapolation PSNR on Dynamic Objects—and there is no parameter-matched time MLP, recurrent model, spline, or other continuous-time baseline. Consequently, the evidence supports the complete architecture more strongly than the claim that learned differential equations are the key source of extrapolation.

Material concern: evidence on real motion is mixed. On PanopticSports, the average PSNR advantage over GaussianPrediction is only about 0.28 dB, and ParticleGS has worse LPIPS on all six sequences. The chosen 90/10 temporal split tests only short-horizon extrapolation, and the authors explicitly select sequences whose motion remains predictable. Horizon-wise curves or evaluations at several train/test cutoffs would better substantiate stable extrapolation.

Material concern: PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS conflate reconstruction quality, appearance, view synthesis, and motion accuracy, as the paper itself acknowledges. No trajectory, optical-flow, keypoint, or 3D motion metric is reported, so claims of more accurate or physically plausible dynamics are not directly verified.

Material concern: the experiments report no repeated runs, uncertainty, or significance analysis, despite small differences on the real dataset. Runtime, memory use, Gaussian count, and rendering speed are also absent, preventing assessment of the computational cost of global attention and ODE integration.

Technical and reproducibility details are incomplete. The manuscript does not provide values for several important encoder settings, learning rates, ODE step configuration, or a precise definition of the ablation variants. The affine decomposition described in the appendix is underspecified, and additive rotation R' = R + ΔR does not by itself preserve a valid rotation representation. The stated code link is blank in the submitted PDF.

The optimization protocol is insufficiently explicit about which timestamps contribute to the loss. Equations 3 and 8 do not clearly establish that held-out future frames are excluded from optimization, even though the experimental split implies this. This should be unambiguous for reproducibility.

Presentation refinements: several claims are imprecise or inconsistent with the tables. For example, the text states approximately 0.1 dB gains over Grid4D on Fan and Telescope, whereas the reported gains are 7.41 and 9.26 dB. There are also recurring naming and grammatical errors ('ParticalGS,' 'GSPrediction'), and some qualitative figures are too small for detailed comparison. These issues reduce clarity but are readily correctable and are not the main basis of the rating.

strengths: ParticleGS presents a coherent encoder-evolver-decoder integration of Neural ODEs with dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting. Factorizing the representation into per-Gaussian static features and a compact set of shared dynamic fields is practically useful and keeps rendering reasonably fast (44.3/37.1 FPS on the two reported datasets, versus 51.0/39.6 for TRACE).

The reported extrapolation results are consistently strong. ParticleGS improves PSNR over the best listed baseline from 33.632 to 36.471 on Dynamic Object, 29.476 to 31.103 on Dynamic Indoor, and 33.526 to 36.136 on Dynamic Multipart. It also obtains the best aggregate result on the real FreeGave-GoPro benchmark, including 26.789 PSNR and 0.150 LPIPS.

The evaluation covers four datasets, including synthetic objects, multipart motion, indoor scenes, and real captures. Full per-scene results and numerous qualitative comparisons are provided, and the visual results generally support improved future-position alignment and detail preservation.

The ablations support several architectural choices. Replacing the ODE evolver reduces extrapolation PSNR from 36.471 to 34.551 on Dynamic Object and from 31.103 to 27.455 on Dynamic Indoor; removing the proposed decoder, progressive training, or neighborhood regeneration also degrades performance.
The manuscript is organized clearly, and the supplement gives useful architectural dimensions, neighborhood construction settings, optimization stages, and full quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning physical laws is not established by the formulation or experiments. The time-dependent Neural ODE d(g_t)/dt=f(g_t,t), trained on a single observed trajectory per scene, can itself memorize that trajectory; an ODE parameterization does not guarantee physical identification or extrapolation. No governing quantity, recovered law, conservation property, force response, or physically meaningful error is evaluated.

The claimed distinction from time-conditioned deformation is theoretically overstated. Because the evolver explicitly receives time and the paper does not demonstrate that the latent state is sufficient under interventions, the assertions that Z_t contains the entire history and provides a physically meaningful Markov state are unsupported. The toy experiment does not resolve this issue because architectures, capacities, optimization, and repeated-run results are omitted, making the comparison difficult to assess.

The particle-system interpretation is weak. All Gaussians receive the same broadcast global dynamic fields, while their static features remain fixed; the rollout contains no explicit particle interactions, spatially varying field evaluation, or feedback from the evolving Gaussian configuration. Thus the method is more accurately a global latent-trajectory model with particle-conditioned decoding than a learned particle dynamics system.

Equation (10) appears technically incorrect as written: x_t=x+Rod(R)x+T maps x to 2x+T when R=0, so the nominal zero-motion transformation is not the identity. A rigid update would normally be Rod(R)x+T, or an additive displacement using (Rod(R)-I)x. This ambiguity directly affects the stated decoder and must be resolved.

Evaluation uses only one 75/25 temporal split. There are no error-versus-horizon curves, substantially longer rollouts, irregular-time tests, altered initial conditions, or perturbation tests. These are especially important for distinguishing learned dynamics from smooth continuation. On the real benchmark, the aggregate PSNR advantage over FreeGave is only 0.279 dB, and no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish its robustness.

Several ablation claims exceed their evidence. The factorized-encoding experiment reports no memory or runtime measurements despite making an efficiency claim, omits the indoor dataset, and uses different hardware. The MLP replacement is insufficiently specified, so it is unclear whether the comparison controls for temporal integration and rollout structure. Likewise, calling Rodrigues-based rotation 'physical decoding' does not by itself demonstrate physical plausibility.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript provides no stated code release and omits learning rates, loss weighting details, time normalization and RK4 step configuration, precise tensor organization/coupling inside the evolver, and sufficient baseline training details. These omissions could materially affect extrapolation performance.

Overall, the empirical contribution is promising and potentially useful, but the physical-law and high-order-dynamics narrative is not adequately validated, and the apparent transformation error plus limited extrapolation analysis keep the paper near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes beyond observed frames rather than only interpolating within the training interval.

ParticleGS is a coherent encoder-evolver-decoder system. Factorizing the representation into particle-specific static features and a small set of global dynamic fields is computationally motivated and supports competitive rendering speed.

The reported empirical results are substantial: ParticleGS has the best average extrapolation PSNR on all four evaluated datasets, with particularly large gains on the synthetic benchmarks. The evaluation includes recent, relevant baselines such as TRACE and FreeGave, as well as per-scene results and qualitative comparisons.

The component ablations cover the factorized encoding, number of fields, ODE evolver, decoder, progressive training, and neighborhood regularization. The appendix also provides useful architectural and optimization details.
weaknesses: The central claim that ParticleGS learns physical laws is not established. The learned fields have no identified physical meaning, no physical constraints or conservation properties, and no evaluation of forces, trajectories, energy, or other physical quantities. All principal evidence consists of image-similarity metrics over a short held-out temporal segment; better future-frame rendering does not by itself demonstrate physical correctness.

The formulation does not exclude trajectory memorization as claimed. The ODE vector field is explicitly time-dependent, d g_t/dt=f(g_t,t), and is optimized separately for each scene over one observed trajectory. Such a model can encode a time-conditioned trajectory just as the criticized baselines do. The paper provides no intervention, changed-initial-condition, cross-trajectory, irregular-sampling, or substantially longer-horizon experiment that would distinguish learning transferable dynamics from fitting a smooth continuation.

The claimed particle dynamics are structurally weak: the same global dynamic vector is broadcast to every Gaussian, while particle-specific motion is produced by a decoder from static features and that global code. There are no state-dependent particle interactions or evolving local states. Consequently, describing the model as approximating Newtonian or Navier-Stokes dynamics and as learning higher-order particle physics is insufficiently justified.

Equation (10) appears technically incorrect or at least seriously underspecified. It defines x_t=x+Rod(R)x+T, which yields x_t=2x+T when R=0; a rigid transform would normally be Rod(R)x+T, or an additive rotational displacement would use (Rod(R)-I)x. Quaternion normalization and the identity convention for the predicted rotation update are also unspecified. Because this equation defines the decoder used in all experiments, this is more than a cosmetic notation issue unless the implementation differs from the manuscript.

The ODE ablation does not isolate the claimed mechanism. The replacement is only described as an equal-parameter MLP, without stating its inputs, rollout structure, or whether it receives time and state. The toy oscillator likewise uses an underdescribed time-conditioned baseline and a single favorable system. These comparisons cannot establish that continuous integration or higher-order dynamics, rather than architecture or optimization differences, causes the gains.

Evaluation breadth is reasonable in dataset count but weak for the paper's scientific claims. Testing only the final 25% of each same-scene sequence provides no horizon-dependent error curves, stability analysis, robustness across frame rates, or generalization to new initial states. There are also no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or tests of whether improvements survive different temporal splits.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: learning rates and schedules, loss weights, RK4 step size or number of function evaluations, time normalization, positional encoding, batch/view sampling, densification settings, training time, and memory consumption are not reported. The out-of-memory factorization ablation is run on different hardware and gives no actual memory measurements.

The method is potentially useful as a scene-specific extrapolation architecture, but its originality is incremental—primarily combining Neural ODE latent evolution with dynamic 3DGS—and the manuscript repeatedly elevates this architectural choice into unsupported claims of physical grounding. The strong rendering numbers make the work worthwhile, but the conceptual and evidentiary gaps currently outweigh them.

strengths: ParticleGS offers a coherent and useful Encoder–Evolver–Decoder formulation: per-Gaussian static features are combined with compact shared dynamic fields, evolved through a Neural ODE, and decoded into Gaussian translations, rotations, and scale changes. This is a meaningful adaptation of continuous dynamics modeling to efficient 3D Gaussian motion extrapolation.

The empirical results are strong and broad. On extrapolation, ParticleGS improves PSNR over the strongest reported baseline from 33.632 to 36.471 on Dynamic Objects, 29.476 to 31.103 on Dynamic Indoor Scenes, and 33.526 to 36.136 on Dynamic Multipart; it also obtains a smaller but consistent aggregate gain on the real-world FreeGave-GoPro data. Qualitative examples generally show better future position and appearance.

The evaluation covers four datasets, synthetic and real scenes, multiple baseline families, reconstruction and extrapolation metrics, per-scene results, and rendering speed. The method remains interactive at 37–44 FPS and therefore offers practical value beyond accuracy alone.

The ablations substantiate the architectural choices. Replacing the ODE evolver reduces extrapolation PSNR from 36.471 to 34.551 and from 31.103 to 27.455 on the two main datasets; factorization, physical decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood regeneration also provide measurable benefits.

The manuscript is well organized, visually clear, and supplies useful implementation information about network dimensions, neighborhood construction, optimization phases, training iterations, and the RK4 solver.
weaknesses: The evidence supports effective extrapolation but not the stronger claim that the model learns physical laws or ensures physical consistency. Evaluation uses only image-quality metrics and selected renderings; it includes no trajectory, geometry, conservation, constraint-violation, or other physical-consistency measurements. The latent variables are also not identified with physical quantities.

The conceptual distinction from time-conditioned deformation is overstated. The proposed derivative network is explicitly fevolver(g_t,t), so time remains an input, and a latent Neural ODE can fit a training trajectory without recovering its governing physics. The toy comparison against x=F(t) lacks architecture, capacity, and training details and does not rule out this explanation.

The mathematical description of physical decoding appears inconsistent: Eq. 10 uses x_t=x+Rod(R)x+T, while the supplement defines Rod(R) as a full rotation matrix. At zero predicted rotation this gives x_t=2x+T, rather than the identity transformation. The intended expression may be Rod(R)x+T or x+(Rod(R)-I)x+T, but this ambiguity is material for correctness and reproducibility.

The assertion that the latent first-order ODE captures higher-order dynamics is an expressivity argument rather than demonstrated behavior. The latent state is not constrained or verified to contain successive derivatives, and the ODE-versus-MLP ablation establishes an architectural advantage, not that higher-order physical dynamics were learned.

Evaluation is limited to a fixed 75%/25% temporal split. There is no accuracy-versus-horizon or substantially longer rollout experiment, which is especially important for claims of stable extrapolation. Several per-scene results are also not best, including Fan, Hyperbolic, Wrist Rest, and some Satellite metrics, while no variation across random seeds or uncertainty is reported.

Reproduction would benefit from learning rates, loss weights, temporal normalization, RK4 step/substep settings, parameter counts, training time, and complete baseline configuration details. These omissions are presentation/reproducibility issues rather than reasons by themselves to reject the otherwise well-supported empirical contribution.
